title: I Was a Teenage Lesbian

jokes.text: Hank launches into rhapsodic description of his perfect morning — breeze, birds, sunshine — then reveals the centerpiece was 'the most incredible dump' he's had since Reagan was in the White House.
jokes.setup: Hank opens with lyrical, almost spiritual language about his perfect morning — the breeze, the birds, the sun shining — building a tone of genuine contentment.
jokes.punchline: The crescendo of this idyllic morning is that he had the greatest bowel movement since the Reagan administration.
jokes.explanation: A textbook misdirection with a beautifully extended setup. Hank's pompous self-importance makes the bathroom reveal land harder — only Hank Kingsley would describe a bowel movement with such reverence and presidential-era specificity. The Reagan timestamp adds historical absurdism that elevates it above a simple gross-out joke. Strong opener that immediately re-establishes the character.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I just took the most incredible dump. I mean, I haven't had one like that since-- I believe-- Reagan was in the White House.

jokes.text: Hank hears his agent Sidney is in intensive care after a heart attack, then immediately pivots to: 'I knew it. Bad things come in threes. First my divorce, then the pool filter catching on fire, and now this.'
jokes.setup: Hank receives genuinely alarming news that his elderly agent may be dying and expresses shock.
jokes.punchline: His 'bad things in threes' list places his agent's potential death as the third item alongside his divorce and a pool filter fire — the bathos of the pool filter is the gut punch.
jokes.explanation: The joke is brilliant because it reveals everything about Hank's character: his self-absorption is so total that a man's potential death is merely one data point in a list about Hank's own suffering, sandwiched between petty personal inconveniences. 'Pool filter catching on fire' is perfectly specific and perfectly trivial. High character integration score — this could only be Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Bad things coming in threes. First my divorce, then the pool filter catching on fire, and now this.

jokes.text: Paula ignores a good morning greeting, Beverly repeats it, and Paula snaps: 'God! Don't be a prick about it.'
jokes.setup: Beverly offers a cheerful good morning greeting twice, totally innocuously.
jokes.punchline: Paula, clearly in a foul mood for unknown reasons, responds to basic human courtesy with 'God! Don't be a prick about it.'
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the complete disproportionality — the gentlest possible greeting provoking genuine aggression. Works as a quick character establishment beat. Economy is the strength here; the whole joke lands in one line.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Hmm? I said good morning. Ok. God! Don't be a prick about it.

jokes.text: 'Oh look. Bitch Expo '95 is in town. Could you pick me up a tee shirt?'
jokes.setup: Two staff members observe Paula's conspicuously terrible mood as she passes through the office.
jokes.punchline: One of them has coined an impromptu name for her current state — 'Bitch Expo '95' — and makes the absurd convention-merchandise request.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable and original. The 'Expo' framing is a genuinely funny construction — turning a mood into a branded corporate event. The tee-shirt add-on commits to the bit. Economy is exceptional; the entire joke is one sentence. Loses points on character integration because it could be delivered by almost any snarky background character.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Oh, look. Bitch expo '95 is in town. Could you pick me up a tee shirt, ok?

jokes.text: Phil is furious about writing an NYPD Blue sketch and demands to know if Jimmy Smits is confirmed: 'Is your grandmother alive? Well, fuck her. I'll get to Jimmy Smits when I get to it.'
jokes.setup: Phil is complaining that he's written an NYPD Blue sketch that was 'painful enough' and needs to know if Jimmy Smits is confirmed so the work wasn't wasted.
jokes.punchline: When asked about his grandmother, Phil establishes she's alive, then uses her existence as the punchline of his dismissal: 'Well, fuck her.'
jokes.explanation: The non-sequitur pivot to the grandmother is genuinely surprising and makes no logical sense, which is the point. Phil's frustration has metastasized into complete irrationality. The line 'Well, fuck her' as a response to the grandmother being alive is dark and absurdist in equal measure. The joke's randomness is its strength — it conveys a writer's mind that has snapped under bureaucratic pressure.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Is your grandmother alive? What? Is she alive? Yes. Well, fuck her. I'll get to Jimmy Smits when I get to it.

jokes.text: Paula reveals she has a lump in her breast, then immediately adds: 'No-no-no. Don't hug, because then it feels serious and cancerous. And please stop staring at my tits.'
jokes.setup: Paula drops a serious, emotionally vulnerable piece of news — she has a lump in her breast.
jokes.punchline: Rather than allowing any emotional moment, she immediately pre-empts the hug ('then it feels serious and cancerous') and follows with the absurd command to stop staring.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional dark comedy execution. 'Then it feels serious and cancerous' is a brilliant psychological insight played for a laugh — the character is managing her own fear through denial of sentiment, and the line articulates that suppression with perfect economy. The pivot to 'stop staring at my tits' adds a layer of absurdist irreverence. This is the kind of joke that only works in a show with this level of character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: I have a lump in my breast.

jokes.text: Paula explains her biopsy is today, admits the waiting is driving her crazy, but insists: 'It's not just the fact that I might die, but my doctor said I can't have coffee anymore. She said it could be a caffeine fibroid tumor. It's turning me into a colossal bitch.'
jokes.setup: Paula has just revealed she has a breast lump and may be dying, and Beverly asks how she's holding up.
jokes.punchline: Her two concerns are, in order: (1) she might die, and (2) she can't have coffee, which is the bigger problem because it's making her mean.
jokes.explanation: The bathos of placing 'might die' and 'can't have coffee' in equal moral weight is characteristic Larry Sanders territory — real human emotion undercut by absurd self-involvement. It also retroactively recontextualizes her earlier moodiness (Bitch Expo '95), making it funnier in retrospect.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Don't hug, because then it feels serious and cancerous.

jokes.text: Larry is in the middle of a massage, and Phil tries to slip him monologue jokes by sliding them under the massage table, then Larry asks him to look through a hole and Phil's thumb blocks the view — escalating awkwardness of conducting show business through a massage table.
jokes.setup: Larry is getting a massage and doesn't want to move, but needs to review Phil's monologue jokes.
jokes.punchline: The solution — sliding papers under the table, peering through a 'hole' — becomes a logistical comedy of errors with Phil's thumb obscuring the view.
jokes.explanation: A solid physical comedy bit that speaks to Larry's entitled comfort-seeking and the indignity of his writers working around it. The escalation is gentle but functional. Works better visually than in transcript form.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: And please stop staring at my tits.

jokes.text: Larry on the massage table: 'Is that Newt Gingrich on the internet?' — 'No, what she's doing to my back. That is great.'
jokes.setup: Phil is with Larry during his massage and presumably makes some reference or sound; Larry seemingly misunderstands who's being referenced.
jokes.punchline: The 'Newt Gingrich' turn is a misdirection — Larry isn't commenting on news, he's comparing the masseuse's technique to something scandalous on the internet, then pulling back to say it's great.
jokes.explanation: A quick topical gag referencing mid-90s internet scandal culture (Newt Gingrich). The misdirection is clean but the joke is a bit loose in the transcript — context-dependent on the visual.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: It's not just the fact that I might die, but my doctor said I can't have coffee anymore... It's turning me into a colossal bitch.

jokes.text: Phil, uncomfortable watching Larry's oily massage, announces he's leaving: 'I was just getting ready to turn over, and sometimes the towel flips up. I've already seen that.' Phil exits.
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to keep Phil engaged during the massage, teasing that he's about to turn over.
jokes.punchline: Phil's deadpan 'I've already seen that' — implying he's witnessed Larry's accidental nudity before — and his immediate departure.
jokes.explanation: A neat cringe beat. 'I've already seen that' does a lot of work: it implies a history of Larry's exhibitionist carelessness, and Phil's world-weary acceptance of it says everything about the toxicity of working in this environment. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I'll look through this hole...

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Is that close enough?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Is that your thumb?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What is that?

jokes.text: Brett Butler drops by during Larry's massage, Larry doesn't recognize the voice but then greets her warmly; Brett's father is there too, Larry greets him with 'Hey, dad. Asshole.'
jokes.setup: Larry is face-down on the massage table when Brett Butler and presumably her father enter. Larry can't see them.
jokes.punchline: Larry greets Brett's father with 'Hey, dad. Asshole.' — suggesting he's met the father before under unflattering circumstances, or it's Larry's casual nickname for him.
jokes.explanation: The casual 'Asshole' as a greeting to a guest's father is a quick left-field gag. Works on the novelty of the insult-as-term-of-endearment in the showbiz world, where everyone is on these first-name-plus-insult terms. Light but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Is that newt gingrich on the internet?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, what she's doing to my back.

jokes.text: Artie interrupts the massage wanting to try the masseuse's elbow technique on Larry's back. He does it, and Larry's immediate pained response — coughing, gasping — prompts Artie to ask: 'What, were you in Vietnam?'
jokes.setup: Artie wants to try the masseuse's elbow technique. Larry says please. Artie applies it.
jokes.punchline: Larry's coughing, gagging reaction to Artie's apparently brutal elbow leads Artie to respond, completely undisturbed, with 'What, were you in Vietnam?'
jokes.explanation: The Vietnam punchline is perfectly Artie — a Vietnam-era tough-guy non-sequitur delivered with complete serenity as Larry suffers. It's a strong character integration moment; the joke works because it requires Artie's specific generational bravado and total indifference to Larry's pain.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I was just getting ready to turn over, and sometimes the towel flips up.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I've already seen that.

jokes.text: Staff member panics that Beverly left Larry's office door 'completely vulnerable' during his massage. Another says Brett Butler is in there. First response: 'I think Brett Butler's in there.' — which immediately deflates the urgency.
jokes.setup: Artie is furious that Beverly abandoned her post outside Larry's office during his sensitive massage time, leaving it open to anyone.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that the intruder is merely Brett Butler — a known, harmless guest — immediately punctures Artie's paranoid security concern.
jokes.explanation: A functional beat that deflates Artie's paranoia. Mild comedy, serves scene-setting purposes more than pure comedic goals.

dialogue.line: Hey, dad.
Asshole.

jokes.text: 'Oh, damn. The day can turn to shit so quickly.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just discovered the office situation isn't actually a crisis — it's Brett Butler.
jokes.punchline: His resigned, almost philosophical observation about the volatility of the day is undercut by the fact that nothing that bad has actually happened.
jokes.explanation: A lovely Artie line — weary, weathered, perfectly delivered in the moment. The irony is that the day hasn't turned to shit at all, which makes his fatalism funnier. Very efficient; works entirely in the economy of the delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What, were you in vietnam?

jokes.text: Artie enters massage room, greets Brett Butler: 'You know, when people ask me who put the best sitcom on the tube last year, you know what I tell them? The butler did it.'
jokes.setup: Artie enters and warmly greets Brett Butler, building up to a compliment about her show.
jokes.punchline: 'The butler did it' — playing on Brett Butler's last name and the old mystery cliché.
jokes.explanation: A charming, old-school pun that fits perfectly in Artie's character voice — he's the kind of man who has a well-worn pun ready for every occasion. The character integration is the strength: this joke belongs to Artie. The pun itself is not novel but it's delivered with the right showbiz panache.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I think Brett Butler's in there.

jokes.text: Brett Butler asks how Artie comes up with that stuff. Artie: 'Oh, my gifts are many and best not discussed.'
jokes.setup: Brett compliments Artie's wit after his 'butler did it' pun.
jokes.punchline: Artie's response is magnificent false modesty: 'My gifts are many and best not discussed' — refusing to explain his wit while simultaneously boasting about it.
jokes.explanation: This is among the best lines in the episode. The phrase 'my gifts are many and best not discussed' is genuinely quotable, original, and perfectly encapsulates Artie's character — a man of enormous ego wrapped in the mannerisms of an elder statesman. It's a paradox (bragging while affecting humility) executed with perfect economy. High character integration: only Artie speaks this way. Justifiably scores above 8.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, damn. The day can turn to shit so quickly.

jokes.text: Larry complains about the rug. Brett Butler asks to 'peek under the towel one more time.' Artie: 'Oh, bretty, you'll dream tonight.'
jokes.setup: The massage scene wraps up with Brett Butler and Artie making their exit, but Brett makes a joking bid to see under Larry's towel.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'You'll dream tonight' — a gallant but absurd implication that a glimpse of Larry's backside would be a fantasy experience.
jokes.explanation: A fun bit of bawdy interplay. Artie's over-the-top endorsement of Larry's physical appeal while Larry is oily and face-down on a table is mildly absurdist. The showbiz flirtation energy is well-captured.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The Butler did it.

jokes.text: Brett Butler to Artie on how she handles fame: 'Just buy bigger shovels and cry sometimes.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks how Brett is handling all the 'horseshit' that fame has brought her.
jokes.punchline: 'Just buy bigger shovels and cry sometimes.' — accepting the shit metaphor and extending it while adding the unexpected emotional note of crying.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Buy bigger shovels and cry sometimes' is exceptional for its economy and emotional intelligence — it takes Artie's horseshit metaphor and extends it practically (bigger shovels) while pivoting to genuine darkness (crying). It's the kind of line that sounds like lived experience. Maximum funny per word. Highly quotable, genuine wit.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: How do you come up with that stuff?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, my gifts are many and best not discussed.

jokes.text: Artie shares Brando's tabloid advice: 'Just tell yourself that everything they write about you is true. That way it won't bother you.'
jokes.setup: Artie is offering Brett Butler wisdom about dealing with tabloid coverage, attributing it to Marlon Brando.
jokes.punchline: The advice is paradoxical — accept the worst about yourself as true — which is both genuinely useful and deeply nihilistic.
jokes.explanation: The Brando name-drop is earned here because the philosophy is genuinely interesting — it's not a random celebrity reference but a specific piece of dark, Brando-appropriate wisdom. The advice is funny because it's simultaneously terrible and helpful. Artie's casual authority ('Here's what Brando told me...') is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Can I just peek under the towel one more time real quick?

jokes.text: Hank delivers a pompous eulogy about the 'bloodsuckers' and 'leeches' coming while Sidney lies on his deathbed — while himself already processing who his new agent will be.
jokes.setup: Hank rails against the indecency of agents swarming while Sidney is dying.
jokes.punchline: The entire speech is hypocritical because Hank is himself planning to replace Sidney and has allowed the ICM agents into the building.
jokes.explanation: The irony is functional but the scene takes too long to land its punchline. The joke is Hank's obliviousness to his own hypocrisy, which is the show's bread and butter, but it's not the sharpest execution of that theme.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, Bretty, you'll dream tonight.

jokes.text: Brett Butler tells Artie she and Paula had 'a thing' ten years ago. Artie chuckles and says 'I thought you'd laugh more.' Brett: 'I did, too.' Then: 'You're uncomfortable.' Artie: 'Hey... I've always loved women with a touch of Sappho.'
jokes.setup: Brett reveals she and Paula had a lesbian relationship in college, expecting Artie to laugh more.
jokes.punchline: Artie's affected open-mindedness — 'I've always loved women with a touch of Sappho' — is both genuinely charming and a subtle admission that he's processing something unexpected.
jokes.explanation: 'Women with a touch of Sappho' is a wonderfully Artie construction — educated, literary, self-consciously worldly, and also slightly performative. The setup of 'I thought you'd laugh more / I did, too' is also a nice bit of shared meta-awareness between the characters. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Just buy bigger shovels and cry sometimes.

jokes.text: Artie: 'We have k.d. lang on the show all the time. Although, the last time, Hank kept calling her 'sir.' That asshole.'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to demonstrate the show's comfort with lesbian/queer guests.
jokes.punchline: The k.d. lang anecdote undercuts the progressive claim: Hank was calling her 'sir,' and Artie dismisses him with 'that asshole' — simultaneously condemning and celebrating Hank as the show's eternal embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. It works on multiple levels: (1) Hank's specific obliviousness about k.d. lang is pitch-perfect character comedy, (2) 'that asshole' is the perfect capper — Artie's fond exasperation with Hank is the show's emotional core, (3) it drops a real celebrity name with an actual comedic payload (not just a name-drop). The joke is efficiently delivered and loaded with character specificity. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Just tell yourself that everything they write about you is true. That way it won't bother you.

jokes.text: Artie on Paula and Brett's past: 'Just because you done it once doesn't make you a dyke.'
jokes.setup: Artie is reassuring Brett (and himself) that the past lesbian encounter doesn't define Paula.
jokes.punchline: His blunt, completely unsophisticated delivery of this 'wisdom' is itself the joke — Artie's version of enlightenment is still very much of its era.
jokes.explanation: Artie's old-school bluntness is always funny, but the phrasing here is more crude than clever. Works as a character moment but doesn't reach the heights of his better lines. The economy is good — he's essentially condensing a Kinsey scale debate into one sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: A man is lying on his deathbed not 5 miles from here, and these bloodsuckers, these leeches... A little respect for the soon-to-be dead, please.

jokes.text: 'Sid was not from the old school. He was from the school they tore down to build the old school.'
jokes.setup: The ICM agents are diplomatically criticizing Sidney as being too old-fashioned, conceding 'If I had to say anything bad about Sid, it would be that he was from the old school.'
jokes.punchline: The other agent tops it: 'He was from the school they tore down to build the old school.'
jokes.explanation: The best pure joke construction in the episode. The first line sets up a well-worn idiom ('old school'), and the second line performs a linguistic inversion that extends the metaphor while amplifying the insult exponentially. 'The school they tore down to build the old school' is an instant quotable — the kind of line a comedy writer would put on their résumé. Perfect structure, maximum economy, genuinely novel. Justifiably above 8.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: I guess you'd call it a lesbian thing.

jokes.text: Hank announces he's having dinner at Spago's with 'that partner from C.A.A.' — implying he's double-booking agent meetings while eulogizing Sidney.
jokes.setup: The ICM agents have just invited Hank to a meal to discuss representation. Hank is performing loyalty to Sidney.
jokes.punchline: He's already booked Spago's with C.A.A. — suggesting the 'bloodsuckers' he just lamented are already his dinner companions.
jokes.explanation: Solidly ironic. The joke is structural — Hank has been performing grief-loyalty while already deep in the replacement process. Works as a character reveal beat.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I've always loved women with a touch of sappho.

jokes.text: Hank on the phone tells Jim from UTA that Sidney is 'dead. Or — or near-dead.'
jokes.setup: Hank is calling yet another agency to begin his agent search while Sidney is still technically alive.
jokes.punchline: 'He's dead. Or — or near-dead.' — the self-correction reveals Hank accidentally committed to a more expedient version of reality, then partially walked it back.
jokes.explanation: A sublimely dark character moment. The slip — 'He's dead' — and the stammered correction reveal that Hank's subconscious has already killed Sidney for the sake of convenience. The correction doesn't rehabilitate him; it makes it worse. Deeply Hank. High character integration — this exact moral failure is uniquely Hank Kingsley. The economy of the moment is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: We have k.d. lang on the show all the time. Although, the last time, Hank kept calling her 'sir.' That asshole.

jokes.text: Brett Butler's cold pre-interview with Paula ends. Brett mutters to herself: 'Cold little bitch.'
jokes.setup: Paula has given Brett a perfunctory, distracted pre-interview and left abruptly.
jokes.punchline: Brett's sotto voce 'Cold little bitch' — a reaction beat that acknowledges the weirdness while being unexpectedly blunt.
jokes.explanation: A quick, satisfying button on an awkward scene. The economy is its strength — three words deliver the entire audience POV. Reasonable character integration: Brett's directness is already established.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Just because you done it once doesn't make you a dyke.

jokes.text: Larry complains about the masseuse: 'You know, she couldn't give me a good massage because half the time her tongue got caught up in her hands.'
jokes.setup: Larry is annoyed that Beverly wasn't there to screen people from his massage, and the masseuse talked too much.
jokes.punchline: The absurdist/literal image of the tongue getting 'caught up in her hands' while massaging is a peculiarly vivid complaint.
jokes.explanation: A nicely specific complaint. The image of the tongue and hands interfering with each other is an original way to describe an overly chatty masseuse. Larry's hyperbolic complaints about minor inconveniences are a character staple and this is a good example.

dialogue.line: Sid was not from the old school. He was from the school they tore down to build the old school.

jokes.text: Brett: 'It'll be like Regis and Kathy Lee. / Artie: 'Just talk about Cody.'
jokes.setup: Brett is panicking that her pre-interview with Paula was inadequate and she and Larry will be misaligned on the show.
jokes.punchline: The Regis and Kathy Lee comparison is the setup; Artie's deadpan 'just talk about Cody' is the punchline — a reference to the notorious Gifford habit of discussing her son Cody Gifford, treated by Artie as a universal fail-safe.
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry-insider callback to a widely recognized television trope. 'Just talk about Cody' is a great deadpan solution — Artie's complete unsentimental pragmatism is perfectly captured. Period-specific but earned.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He's dead. Or-- or near-dead.

jokes.text: 'Sid wasn't from the old school. Sid was from the school they tore down to build the old school.' [Delivered again to Larry; everyone laughs.]
jokes.setup: The ICM agents' joke about Sidney is being retold to the group in the main office.
jokes.punchline: The repetition of the line — now performed for a larger audience — works as a callback that also reveals how instantly it's entered the office's collective consciousness.
jokes.explanation: The callback is earned because the line is genuinely good enough to repeat. Its second telling is almost more revealing than the first — Hank repeating an insult against his dying agent's reputation within the same hour is its own dark joke. Scored lower than the original because the structural innovation is already done.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Cold little bitch.

jokes.text: Artie on the C.A.A. agents: 'You get those bastards out of my studio, Hank. If they find a hole anywhere, they'll either fuck it or build a nest in it.'
jokes.setup: Artie is dismissing the C.A.A. agents who've been circling Hank.
jokes.punchline: 'Either fuck it or build a nest in it' — an extremely vivid and original metaphor for predatory Hollywood agent behavior.
jokes.explanation: The single best line of the episode. 'They'll either fuck it or build a nest in it' is a genuinely remarkable piece of writing — a maximally vivid, completely original metaphor for Hollywood opportunism. It's both crude and precise; it captures the predatory, territorial nature of talent agencies in a way that no other formulation could. Only Artie says things like this, and only in this show. Rip Torn delivering this line in character is TV-comedy gold. Justifiably 8+; close to a 9.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know, she couldn't give me a good massage because half the time her tongue got caught up in her hands.

jokes.text: Artie tells Paula he was 'about to give her a swift kick in the anny-fey' before learning about her lump.
jokes.setup: Artie enters to reprimand Paula for her unprofessionalism with Brett Butler.
jokes.punchline: 'A swift kick in the anny-fey' — Artie's folksy, archaic euphemism for the backside (likely a Rip Torn improv or period-specific regional phrase).
jokes.explanation: 'Anny-fey' is a deliberately quaint, Artie-specific piece of colorful language. Its contrast with his otherwise blunt vocabulary is funny. The character integration is high because this kind of archaic colloquialism belongs specifically to Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: It'll be like Regis and Kathy Lee.

jokes.text: Paula says she's not comfortable discussing her 'bosom' with Artie. Artie says he knows what she's going through because 20 years ago he found a lump on one of his testicles.
jokes.setup: Paula wants privacy around her medical situation; Artie is bridging it with empathy.
jokes.punchline: His empathy bridge turns out to be a testicular lump story — connecting Paula's breast lump to his own experience in a way that is both generous and completely tone-deaf.
jokes.explanation: Artie's brand of empathy is always simultaneously touching and oblivious. Here the joke is in the parallel — he draws a genuine connection between their experiences while also being unaware that the specifics of his example (testicles vs. breast) creates a new awkwardness. This is the show's emotional register at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I found a lump on one of my testicles... I made Elke Sommer cry in the middle of a dance rehearsal.

jokes.text: Artie's testicle lump story: 'I was doing a Bob Hope special at the time... I let it affect my work. I made Elke Summer cry in the middle of a dance rehearsal. I'm not proud of that.'
jokes.setup: Artie is recounting how his testicular scare affected his work on a Bob Hope special.
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of making 'Elke Summer cry in the middle of a dance rehearsal' — this is an absurdly specific vintage Hollywood casualty of his emotional breakdown.
jokes.explanation: Elke Sommer (the actress) as an unexpected collateral casualty of Artie's testicular anxiety is a brilliant specificity. The period detail grounds the character and makes him feel like a man with a genuinely strange life. 'I'm not proud of that' — delivered with complete sincerity — is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Because he was thinking about my left nut.

jokes.text: Artie concludes his testicle story with a lesson for Paula: 'I told Bob about the lump the day before we taped. The monologue died. Bob's timing went on a shit. You know why? Because he was thinking about my left nut.'
jokes.setup: Artie is building to his moral — don't let personal crises affect professional performance.
jokes.punchline: The explanation for Bob Hope's failed timing: 'Because he was thinking about my left nut.' A sentence that has no right to be as funny as it is.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best in the series. The specificity of 'my LEFT nut' is genuinely inspired — if it were just 'my nut,' it would be half as funny. The premise that Bob Hope's professional comedy timing was derailed by empathetic distraction about Artie's specific left testicle is an escalation that shouldn't work but lands perfectly. The sentence is structured with perfect comic rhythm. It's spoken as solemn wisdom, making it funnier. This is what an exceptional Larry Sanders line looks like: Rip Torn, mid-career, at the top of his game. Justified score above 9.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That's the show I fucked up because of my titty.

jokes.text: Artie tells Paula: 'Because 20 years from now, you don't want to be watching a Larry Sanders rerun and have to say, "Oh, yeah. That's the show I fucked up because of my titty."'
jokes.setup: Artie is delivering the moral of his testicle story — a warning not to let personal medical crisis affect work.
jokes.punchline: The word 'titty' as the capper to an otherwise solemn speech — and the absurd image of Paula in her old age watching a Sanders rerun and being haunted by it.
jokes.explanation: The word 'titty' used in a solemn professional-advice context is funny on its own, but what makes this great is the specific scenario: imagining Paula decades from now watching the exact rerun of this show. It's almost meta-self-referential (a character on The Larry Sanders Show is warned not to ruin The Larry Sanders Show). The structure is perfect — earnest wisdom delivered in Artie's most avuncular register, then punctuated with 'titty.' This is exceptional comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Just go straight up your ass and turn left.

jokes.text: Staff member's response to someone asking where Hank Kingsley's office is: 'Uh, yeah. Just go straight up your ass and turn left.'
jokes.setup: Someone (a C.A.A. agent) asks an office staffer where Hank Kingsley's office is.
jokes.punchline: The staffer's contempt for the agents is total: 'Just go straight up your ass and turn left.'
jokes.explanation: A very satisfying insult that captures the staff's contempt for Hollywood agents descending on the office during a crisis. The directional specificity ('turn left') makes a crude insult into something more deliberate and funny. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You're not all getting on the elevator at once, are you? You kids, you're so crazy!

jokes.text: Hank ushers C.A.A. agents out of the studio, joking: 'You're not all getting on the elevator at once, are you? You kids, you're so crazy!'
jokes.setup: Hank is managing his awkward position — pretending loyalty to Sidney while having multiple agent meetings.
jokes.punchline: His obsequious, performatively jovial way of ushering people out — 'you kids, you're so crazy!' — is the kind of hollow showbiz glad-handing that reveals his desperation.
jokes.explanation: Functional Hank character comedy — his desperate likability-management is well-captured. Not one of the sharper moments but consistent with the episode's portrait of him.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It was a hiatal hernia. It's a rip in the esophagus... Fucking doctors! I mean, come on!

jokes.text: Hank herds the ICM agents to the elevator: 'You're not all getting on the elevator at once, are you? You kids, you're so crazy!' — performing warmth for people he's just had ejected.
jokes.setup: Hank has just received orders from Artie to get the agents out and is escorting them to the elevator.
jokes.punchline: The performative bonhomie — 'You kids, you're so crazy!' — while simultaneously pushing them out the door reveals Hank's complete comfort with transparent insincerity.
jokes.explanation: A nice Hank beat. His inability to be openly rude — even when trying to eject people — combined with his showbiz reflex warmth is perfectly calibrated character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: If you say a person's not going to make it through the day, then he shouldn't make it. It's just so inconsiderate to just put us through this worry.

jokes.text: Brian tells Hank that Sid is going to be fine — it wasn't a heart attack, just a hiatal hernia. Hank's response: 'Fucking doctors! I mean, come on!'
jokes.setup: Brian delivers the miraculous good news: Sidney is alive and will recover. It's presented as wonderful.
jokes.punchline: Hank's immediate response is anger at the doctors for the false alarm — completely inverting the expected relief.
jokes.explanation: A spectacular Hank moment. The inversion is perfect — Hank is angry that a man DIDN'T die, and his anger is directed at doctors for 'inconsiderate' false alarms. It is a completely Hank reaction: the emotional inconvenience of hope and grief is what he's objecting to. The reveal follows immediately with even more explicit language about how the patient 'shouldn't have made it through the day' since that's what he was told. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Hank elaborates: 'If you say a person's not going to make it through the day, then he shouldn't make it. It — it's just so inconsiderate to just put us through this worry.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just expressed anger that Sidney survived. He now explains his position more fully.
jokes.punchline: His moral framework: if a doctor gives a terminal prognosis, the patient has a social obligation to die on schedule. Sidney has been 'inconsiderate.'
jokes.explanation: This is Hank at his most magnificent and monstrous. The complaint — that Sidney's survival is 'inconsiderate' — is one of the most perfectly articulated expressions of Hank's bottomless self-absorption in the entire series. The logic is impeccable within Hank's worldview: he arranged his emotions (and his agent search) around a death that didn't come, and this is Sidney's fault. This is Tambor-level character comedy at its peak. Very close to the SNip, Snap calibration benchmark for character-specific escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: So I say, 'hoist another cup of joe to lumpy.'

jokes.text: Hank, after his outburst, pivots to weeping: 'I'm so happy.' Then: 'Call the guys at C.A.A. and tell 'em... maybe in a couple years.' Then collapses into tears again: 'I'm so happy.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just expressed fury and resentment at Sidney's survival.
jokes.punchline: He pivots on a dime to tearful happiness — while in the same breath instructing his assistant to tell the C.A.A. agents they'll need to wait a couple of years before approaching again.
jokes.explanation: The dual-track of genuine emotion and calculating agent-management is pitch-perfect Hank. He's crying real tears while simultaneously scheduling Sidney's eventual replacement. 'Maybe in a couple years' is the best comedy beat — it's a tentative booking of Sidney's future death. The cycling between 'I'm so happy' and practical agent logistics is beautifully calibrated cringe comedy.

dialogue.line: There's, like, no smoking in the office, dipshit.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Fuck you. I'm, like, alive, dipshit.

jokes.text: Hank in tears after news of Sid's recovery — Brian: 'I know. We're all happy.' Hank weeping and nodding, clearly a mess.
jokes.setup: After the 'I'm so happy' performance, Hank has apparently genuinely broken down.
jokes.punchline: The image of Hank, a grown man in show business, fully weeping over an agent who was apparently fine all along — and Brian's flat 'We're all happy' trying to process this.
jokes.explanation: Jeffrey Tambor's physical comedy is inferred here. The weeping creates a tonal whiplash after Hank's outrage — we don't know if he's crying from relief, grief, or the collapse of his career ambitions. The ambiguity is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Where in goddamn hell is the fire?! You scared the shit out of me!
It's just the incense.

jokes.text: Beverly has her biopsy result — benign fibroid — and jokes: 'So I say, hoist another cup of joe to Lumpy.'
jokes.setup: Beverly has just gotten the relief of a benign biopsy — her lump is a caffeine fibroid, not cancer.
jokes.punchline: Rather than relief, she immediately normalizes it with 'hoist another cup of joe to Lumpy' — toasting her tumor with the substance that caused it.
jokes.explanation: A nice piece of dark relief comedy. 'Lumpy' as a name for the tumor is funny and humanizing; the toast with coffee is a logical absurdity (the thing that caused the lump). Solid mid-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: You are so... unbelievable. You know what I remember 10 years ago? You're very, very selfish.

jokes.text: 'There's, like, no smoking in the office, dipshit.' — 'Fuck you. I'm, like, alive, dipshit.'
jokes.setup: Someone calls out a coworker smoking in the office.
jokes.punchline: 'Fuck you. I'm, like, alive, dipshit' — Beverly (or a colleague) justifying smoking because she just got a clean bill of health — using survival as license for recklessness.
jokes.explanation: The caustic logic of 'I'm alive, so I'm going to celebrate by doing something dangerous' is very dark and very funny. The parallel 'dipshit' structure is a nice comedic mirror. Strong economy — the whole joke is two lines.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I almost lost a-- I almost lost Sid today... Sid, take care of your esophagus.

jokes.text: Artie bursts through a door into what appears to be an aromatherapy/meditation session for Larry, who has fallen off the table: 'Where in goddamn hell is the fire?! You scared the shit out of me!' — 'It's just the incense.' — 'Oh, sorry. God. As you were.'
jokes.setup: Larry is mid-session with what appears to be an intense alternative therapy, and Artie barges in expecting an emergency.
jokes.punchline: The 'fire' Artie thought he smelled is just incense. His military 'As you were' after nearly giving Larry a coronary is the button.
jokes.explanation: 'As you were' after causing chaos is perfectly Artie — he recovers his authority instantly and exits as if nothing happened. The physical comedy of Larry presumably falling off the table ('my nose is bleeding') adds a layer the transcript implies.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: I got a massage. The woman did not stop talking... And plus, she wanted a very steep security and cleaning deposit which I did not get back afterwards.

jokes.text: Brett Butler tells Paula their lesbian thing was 10 years ago and she shouldn't 'spend the rest of her career trying to dodge' her. Paula reveals she's been distracted because she thought she was dying — a tumor in her breast. Brett's relief: 'Oh, Paula, what a relief.' Then Paula: 'I thought you were mad at me.' Brett: [stunned] 'Are you serious? What's wrong?'
jokes.setup: Brett has been trying to clear the air about their past relationship. Paula finally explains she's been worried about dying.
jokes.punchline: Upon learning the tumor is benign, Paula's immediate first thought is relief that Brett isn't mad at her — completely inverting the gravity of the medical situation.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured character revelation. Paula's anxieties are so socially oriented that Brett's opinion outranks her own mortality in her hierarchy of concerns. The audience realizes before Brett does that Paula's 'relief' is about the interpersonal, not the medical. Brett's incredulous 'Are you serious?' does all the necessary work. This earns its score through excellent structural setup and payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: You get your mom a house and you figure whatever else you do with your money is ok if you get your mom a house.

jokes.text: Brett calls Paula 'very, very selfish' for caring more about Brett's opinion than her own cancer scare. Paula retorts: 'Oh, fuck you.' Brett: 'Oh, fuck you, fuck you.' Both burst into laughter.
jokes.setup: Brett has just called out Paula's inverted priorities. The conversation has gotten heated.
jokes.punchline: The mutual 'fuck you' exchange that resolves into shared laughter — the women's genuine history and affection breaking through the surface argument.
jokes.explanation: The laugh that follows 'fuck you, fuck you' earns it a slightly higher score than the exchange alone would merit. It's emotionally true — the quickest way these two can reconnect is through profanity. Not a constructed joke but a character moment with comedic value.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: I'm a WASP. Wasps don't have guilt, do they?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, no. But they have moms.

jokes.text: Larry on air, dedicating a segment to Sidney: 'I almost lost a— I almost lost Sid today. Um, and I almost lost sight of the fact that, uh, I— I almost lost him. So, anyway, uh... Sid, take care of your esophagus.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing a heartfelt on-air tribute to his friend and Hank's agent, Sidney.
jokes.punchline: His tribute collapses into circular, meaningless repetition ('I almost lost him... I almost lost sight of... I almost lost him'), then concludes with the magnificently deflated 'take care of your esophagus.'
jokes.explanation: The verbal stumbling is perfectly Larry — his on-air self-consciousness collides with genuine emotion and produces linguistic chaos. The resolution 'take care of your esophagus' is precisely the kind of anti-climactic wisdom that only a talk show host would deliver as a public statement of love. High character integration: Larry's inability to be sincere without undermining himself is his defining trait.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Hey, see what happens when you mess around with another chick? It's bad news, huh?

jokes.text: Brett Butler on her TV show: 'Boy, you've had a bad day.' Larry: 'I had a horrible day. I got a massage. The woman did not stop talking. Have you ever had that? And plus she wanted a very steep security and cleaning deposit which I did not get back afterwards.'
jokes.setup: Brett is sympathizing with Larry's difficult day (involving a near-death of a friend, emotional turmoil).
jokes.punchline: Larry summarizes his horrible day as: (1) chatty masseuse, (2) didn't get his cleaning deposit back.
jokes.explanation: The irony is rich: Larry had an emotionally complex day involving mortality, agent vultures, lesbian revelations, and a friend's near-death — and on camera he summarizes it as a bad massage and a lost cleaning deposit. Perfect character integration: Larry's vanity and entitlement mean his petty grievances genuinely ARE his bad day. The cleaning deposit detail is wonderfully specific and absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, some dyke thing, I guess.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, it appears I owe you $100.

jokes.text: Brett Butler on her three-bedroom house: 'I do just live in a three-bedroom house, though, so that's not pretentious, is it?' Then: 'You get your mom a house and you figure whatever else you do with your money is ok if you get your mom a house.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Brett what she does with her money from television success.
jokes.punchline: The moral framework: buying your mom a house provides a moral blank check for all other expenditure.
jokes.explanation: A clever piece of celebrity self-mythology — the 'I bought my mom a house' as ultimate virtue signaling that retroactively justifies all excess. Brett delivering it with complete earnestness makes it work. This reads like autobiographical comedy from Brett Butler's actual life, which adds an extra layer.

jokes.text: Larry asks Brett if she feels guilt about her money. Brett: 'I'm a WASP. Why?' Larry: 'WASPs don't have guilt, do they?' Brett: 'Oh, no. But they have moms.'
jokes.setup: Larry is pursuing the guilt angle — whether having money creates moral anxiety.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, no. But they have moms.' — acknowledging the WASP absence of guilt while pivoting to maternal obligation as the substitute mechanism.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely smart observation: WASPs replace guilt with obligation. The structure is clean — setup (WASPs/guilt), punchline (moms as the guilt substitute). The line is memorable and perceptive. Very economical. Larry's offscreen reaction ('y'all killed him') implies the audience loved it, and justifiably — this is professional guest-spot comedy.

jokes.text: Larry (to Artie, post-show): 'I'll tell you the best part of that interview — at no point did she put her elbow in my back.'
jokes.setup: Larry is debriefing the show with Artie, praising Brett Butler's performance.
jokes.punchline: His highest praise for the interview is that Brett Butler did not replicate Artie's earlier assault on his back.
jokes.explanation: A nice callback that ties together the episode's physical comedy thread. The joke is in the inversion — the standard praise for an interview is quality of conversation; Larry's metric is physical non-assault. Good economy and character-specific.

jokes.text: Artie tells Larry he has a 'tale to tell' about Brett Butler and 'our own sweet paula,' adds: 'Prepare to be a god, junior.'
jokes.setup: Artie is teasing Larry with the lesbian backstory between Paula and Brett.
jokes.punchline: 'Prepare to be a god, junior.' — Artie framing gossip as a divine ascension.
jokes.explanation: 'Prepare to be a god, junior' is a wonderful Artie-ism. Only Artie would describe the reception of gossip in mythological terms. The 'junior' adds the right amount of patronizing affection. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Brett apologizes to Paula backstage, admits: 'You're right. I do have my head up my ass.'
jokes.setup: Brett is apologizing for her own behavior in their conversation — trying to clear the air.
jokes.punchline: She agrees with Paula's implicit criticism with unexpected self-awareness: 'I do have my head up my ass.'
jokes.explanation: A functional self-deprecation beat. The directness is refreshing in a show full of indirect people, which gives it some comedic contrast value.

jokes.text: Hank to Paula about the lesbian history: 'Hey, see what happens when you mess around with another chick? It's bad news, huh?' — completely missing the point of why Paula's day was difficult.
jokes.setup: The episode has revealed the Paula/Brett history and resolved their tension; Hank offers his take.
jokes.punchline: Hank interprets the entire day's drama as a cautionary tale about lesbianism, rather than about Paula's cancer scare or the Brett awkwardness.
jokes.explanation: A pitch-perfect Hank beat to close his relationship to the episode's storyline. His takeaway from the whole day is a homophobic non-sequitur that misreads everything. The character integration is near-perfect — the specific wrongness of Hank's analysis is the joke, and it's entirely consistent with every other Hank moment in the episode.

jokes.text: Hank, after being told about the Paula-Brett lesbian backstory, says: 'Well, it appears I owe you $100.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just revealed the lesbian backstory to Larry and (presumably) Hank.
jokes.punchline: Hank's response — 'I owe you $100' — reveals there was a standing bet, or that this information has instantly resolved some long-standing debate or wager in Hank's mind.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button for the episode. 'I owe you $100' implies (1) Hank had an opinion about Paula's sexuality before this, (2) someone bet against it, and (3) Hank is now the loser of that bet with complete equanimity. It's the cleanest possible punchline — maximum information in minimum words. The implication that this is the kind of thing people bet on in the Larry Sanders office is a perfect satire of Hollywood's prurient gossip economy. Excellent final joke.

tmdb_overview: While awaiting the results of a breast biopsy, a tense Paula angers Brett Butler who offers Larry some tips on his weekly massage. Hank interviews possible new agents while his beloved Sid lies gravely ill in the hospital.
